insider_note: A modulus integral is always split at the point where the inside expression is zero — get that point right and the rest is routine integration.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split the modulus using its definition
steps.margin_note: First mark. |1−x| changes sign exactly where 1−x=0, i.e. at x=1 — always split there.
steps.memory_tip: The split point for |a−x| is always x=a.
lines: From the definition of the modulus function,
steps.why: The modulus |1−x| changes its algebraic sign at x=1, so the single integral must be split into two pieces at that point, one for each sign of (1−x).
common_mistakes: Integrating |1−x| as (1−x) over the whole interval without splitting at x=1.
Splitting at the wrong point, e.g. x=0 instead of x=1.

steps.label: Integrate each piece and add
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both pieces contribute exactly 1/2 each — a useful check on the arithmetic.
steps.memory_tip: By symmetry about x=1, the two pieces of a V-shaped modulus graph often contribute equal areas.
steps.why: Integrating each piece over its own interval and adding the two results gives the total area under |1−x| from 0 to 2, which comes out to a clean whole number.
common_mistakes: Sign errors when evaluating the second integral's limits.
Adding the two pieces incorrectly instead of tracking each bracket separately.
